analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Industries is a capital-hungry specialty chemicals manufacturer whose returns on equity have collapsed to 6% while the market still charges 43x earnings — a combination I find nearly impossible to justify. Net profit has cratered from INR 1,186 Cr in 2022 to INR 331 Cr in 2025 as Chinese competition and domestic overcapacity bite.
key_strengths: Revenue has grown at a 10.3% CAGR over nine years, showing genuine long-term scale-up
Operationally cash-flow positive every year for five years (5/5), meaning the base business generates cash before heavy capex
Some long-term supply contracts with MNC pharma and agrochem customers provide visibility
key_risks: ROE of only 6.03% — barely a third of my 15% minimum — despite years of heavy investment
Net profit has fallen 72% in three years (INR 1,186 Cr → INR 331 Cr); EBITDA trend is contracting
Capex of INR 1,300–1,400 Cr annually against EBITDA of ~INR 986 Cr produces persistent negative free cash flow (-INR 137 Cr in 2025)
red_flags: P/E of 43x on sharply declining earnings — the market is pricing a recovery that the financials do not support
Finance costs have risen 27% in two years (INR 211 → INR 275 Cr) while profits collapsed — leverage is going in the wrong direction
CWIP of INR 1,596 Cr (up from INR 1,096 Cr in 2023) signals further heavy spending before any returns materialise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
A wonderful business earns high returns on incremental capital. Aarti Industries is doing precisely the opposite: it has spent over INR 5,000 Cr in capex over four years while net profit fell from INR 1,186 Cr to INR 331 Cr and ROE dropped to 6%. Specialty chemicals can have moats — proprietary processes, customer qualification barriers — but the current numbers offer no evidence of pricing power. Operating margins of 8.8% look thin for a company claiming specialty status.

At 43x trailing P/E the market is betting on a sharp earnings reversal. Even if profits recover to INR 700–800 Cr, the stock would trade at 20–23x on still-mediocre returns on equity. I prefer to own businesses where the numbers already demonstrate the moat, not ones where I must hope management builds it. Aarti Industries fails that test decisively today.
